# Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Obstructive lung diseases > Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/3h0Sdf)

---

## Summary

Chronic <u>obstructive pulmonary disease</u> (COPD) is characterized by chronic respiratory symptoms resulting from airflow obstruction and alveolar <u>gas exchange</u> abnormalities. It is predominantly caused by inhaled toxins (e.g., <u>tobacco smoke</u> or <u>air pollution</u>). Some individuals are genetically predisposed to COPD, particularly those with <u>α<sub>1</sub>-antitrypsin deficiency</u> (<u>AATD</u>). COPD begins with chronic <u>airway</u> inflammation, which usually progresses to <u>emphysema</u>, a condition that is characterized by permanent dilatation of pulmonary air spaces <u>distal</u> to the <u>terminal bronchioles</u>. These changes cause a loss of <u>diffusion</u> area, which can lead to inadequate oxygen absorption (<u>hypoxemia</u>) and CO<sub>2</sub> release (<u>hypercapnia</u>). Clinical features include <u>dyspnea</u> and productive <u>cough</u> and, in later stages, <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, and <u>cyanosis</u>. Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical presentation and <u>pulmonary function tests</u> (<u>PFTs</u>), which typically show a decreased <u>ratio</u> of <u>forced expiratory volume</u> (<u>FEV</u>) to <u>forced vital capacity</u> (<u>FVC</u>). Imaging studies are helpful in assessing disease severity and the extent of possible complications. Treatment options mainly consist of short-acting and long-acting <u>bronchodilators</u> and <u>inhaled corticosteroids</u>. Individuals with advanced disease may benefit from oxygen supplementation and/or <u>noninvasive ventilation</u>. COPD can cause complications such as <u>pulmonary hypertension</u> or <u>respiratory failure</u>. The most significant complication is <u>acute exacerbation of COPD</u>.




![COPD fact sheet](media/mlaaz1gy6esk7cv5gclp6gk7.jpg)

COPD fact sheet

---

## Definitions

* Chronic <u>obstructive pulmonary disease</u>: a <u>lung</u> condition characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms (<u>cough</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>) and airflow limitation (postbronchodilator <u>FEV<sub>1</sub>:FVC ratio</u> < 0.70), which is caused by a combination of small <u>airway obstruction</u> and <u>parenchymal</u> destruction

* Chronic bronchitis: productive <u>cough</u> for at least 3 months per year for 2 consecutive years that cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis

* Emphysema: permanent dilatation of pulmonary air spaces <u>distal</u> to the <u>terminal bronchioles</u> that is caused by the destruction of the alveolar walls and pulmonary <u>capillaries</u> required for <u>gas exchange</u>

* Preserved ratio impaired spirometry (<u>PRISm</u>): A term describing individuals with postbronchodilator <u>FEV<sub>1</sub>:FVC ratio</u> ≥ 0.70 but an <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> < 80% of the predicted value.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Chronic bronchitis</u> (a clinically defined condition) and <u>emphysema</u> (an anatomically defined condition) often occur simultaneously in patients with COPD. [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)

---

## Etiology

### <u>Exogenous</u> factors




* Tobacco use ;  [[6]](/library/U30b3f)

* Smoking is the major <u>risk factor for COPD</u>, but those who have quit ≥ 10 years ago are not at increased risk. [[7]](/library/ZuYZpI)

* <u>Passive smoking</u>

* Exposure to <u>air pollution</u> or fine dusts [[8]](/library/--0D-i)

* Nonorganic dust: such as industrial <u>bronchitis</u> in coal miners [[9]](/library/ZZaZZQ)

* Organic dust: ↑ <u>incidence</u> of COPD in areas where biomass fuel (e.g., wood, animal dung) is regularly burned indoors





### <u>Endogenous</u> factors




* <u>Lung</u> growth and development abnormalities [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)

* Recurrent pulmonary infections and <u>tuberculosis</u>

* <u>Premature birth</u>  [[10]](/library/aubQpv)

* <u>α1-antitrypsin deficiency</u>

* <u>Airway</u> hyperresponsiveness

* <u>Antibody</u> deficiency syndrome (e.g., <u>IgA</u> deficiency)

* <u>Primary ciliary dyskinesia</u> (e.g., <u>Kartagener syndrome</u>)

## Classification

### <u>GOLD classification</u> [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




<u>GOLD spirometric grades</u> inform the prognosis of a patient; <u>GOLD groups</u> guide pharmacological management.




#### GOLD grades




| <br><u>GOLD spirometric grades</u> [[1]](/library/IEdYC70) |  |
| --- | --- |
| Grade | Postbronchodilator <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u>% of the predicted value |
| GOLD 1: mild | ≥ 80% |
| GOLD 2: moderate | 50–79% |
| GOLD 3: severe | 30–49% |
| GOLD 4: very severe | < 30% |





> [!NOTE]
> Cutoff points between <u>GOLD spirometric grades</u> according to the <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u>%: 30 + 50 = 80




#### GOLD groups [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




| <br><u>GOLD group</u> assessment [[1]](/library/IEdYC70) |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Group | <br>Exacerbations in the past year<br> | <br>Severity of symptoms <br> |  |
| <u>mMRC dyspnea scale</u> | <u>CAT score</u> |  |  |
| GOLD group A | <br><br>* 0<br><br>* Or 1 not leading to hospital admission<br><br><br> | <br>* 0–1<br><br> | <br>* 0–9<br><br> |
| GOLD group B | <br>* ≥ 2<br><br> | <br>* ≥ 10<br><br> |  |
| <br>GOLD group E<br> | <br><br>* ≥ 2 moderate exacerbations<br><br>* Or ≥ 1 leading to hospital admission<br><br><br> | <br>* Any severity<br><br> |  |

## Pathophysiology

COPD is characterized by chronic <u>airway</u> inflammation and tissue destruction. [[6]](/library/U30b3f)[[11]](/library/p30Ljf)




### <u>Chronic inflammation</u>




It results from significant exposure to noxious stimuli, increased oxidative <u>stress</u> (most commonly due to <u>cigarette smoke</u>) as well as by increased release of <u>reactive oxygen species</u> by inflammatory cells.




* Increased number of <u>neutrophils</u>, <u>macrophages</u>, and <u>CD8+ T lymphocytes</u> → release of <u>cytokines</u> → amplification of inflammation and induction of structural changes of <u>lung parenchyma</u> (e.g., via stimulation of growth factor release)

* <u>CD8+ T lymphocytes</u> mediate inflammation in individuals with COPD.

* <u>CD4+ T lymphocytes</u> and <u>eosinophils</u> mediate inflammation in individuals with <u>bronchial asthma</u>.

* Overproduction of growth factor → peribronchiolar <u>fibrosis</u> → narrowing of <u>airway</u> → obliteration → <u>emphysema</u> (airflow limitation)

* Promotion of <u>goblet cell</u> <u>proliferation</u> and <u>hypertrophy</u>, mucus hypersecretion, and impaired ciliary function → chronic productive <u>cough</u>

* Reid index is the <u>ratio</u> of the thickness of the <u>submucosal</u> mucus-secreting glands to the thickness between the <u>epithelium</u> and <u>cartilage</u> in the bronchial tree.

* <u>Reid index</u> > 0.5 is characteristic of <u>chronic bronchitis</u>. [[12]](/library/Q9buMD)

* <u>Smooth muscle</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> of the small <u>airways</u> and pulmonary vasculature (mainly due to <u>hypoxic</u> <u>vasoconstriction</u>) → pulmonary <u>hypertension</u> → <u>cor pulmonale</u>





### Tissue destruction [[13]](/library/uiYptK)




* Bronchopulmonary inflammation → ↑ <u>proteases</u>

* <u>Nicotine</u> use (or other noxious stimuli) inactivates <u>protease inhibitors</u> (especially <u>α<sub>1</sub>-antitrypsin</u>) → imbalance of <u>protease</u> and antiprotease → ↑ <u>elastase</u> activity → loss of elastic tissue and <u>lung parenchyma</u> (via destruction of the alveolar walls), which causes:

* Enlargement of airspaces → ↓ elastic recoil and ↑ compliance of the <u>lung</u> → ↓ tethering of small <u>airways</u> → expiratory <u>airway</u> collapse and obstruction → <u>air trapping</u> and hyperinflation → ↓ ventilation (due to air-trapping) and ↑ <u>dead space</u> → ↓ <u>DL<sub>CO</sub></u>and ↑ <u>ventilation-perfusion</u> mismatch (<u>V/Q</u>) → <u>hypoxemia</u> and <u>hypercapnia</u>

* <u>Pulmonary shunt</u> and ↓ blood volume in pulmonary <u>capillaries</u> → ↑ number of <u>alveoli</u> that are ventilated but not <u>perfused</u> (↑ <u>dead space</u>) → ↓ <u>DL<sub>CO</sub></u> and ↑ <u>V/Q</u> → <u>hypoxemia</u> and <u>hypercapnia</u>

* Imbalance of oxidants and anti-oxidants and an overabundance of <u>free radicals</u> → <u>chronic inflammation</u> and inactivation of anti-<u>elastase</u> → breakdown of elastic tissue.





![Pulmonary emphysema](media/rpwr4pq14ufj2y9q076pz3h5.jpg)

## Clinical features

Symptoms are minimal or nonspecific until the disease reaches an advanced stage.




### Presenting findings [[6]](/library/U30b3f)




* <u>Chronic cough</u> with expectoration (expectoration typically occurs in the morning)

* <u>Dyspnea</u> and <u>tachypnea</u>

* Initial stages: only on exertion

* Advanced stages: continuously

* Pursed lip breathing

* The patient breathes in through the nose and breathes out slowly through pursed <u>lips</u>.

* This style of breathing increases <u>airway</u> pressure and prevents bronchial collapse during the last phase of expiration.

* More commonly seen in patients with <u>emphysema</u>

* Prolonged expiratory phase, end-expiratory <u>wheezing</u>, <u>crackles</u>, muffled breath sounds, and/or coarse <u>rhonchi</u> on <u>auscultation</u>

* <u>Cyanosis</u> due to <u>hypoxemia</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>





### Features of advanced COPD [[14]](/library/FVYgwL)




* Congested neck <u>veins</u>

* <u>Barrel chest</u>: This deformity is most commonly seen in individuals with <u>emphysema</u>.

* Asynchronous movement of the chest and abdomen during respiration

* Use of accessory respiratory muscles due to diaphragmatic dysfunction

* Hyperresonant <u>lungs</u>, reduced diaphragmatic excursion, and relative cardiac dullness on percussion

* Decreased breath sounds on <u>auscultation</u>: “silent <u>lung</u>”

* <u>Peripheral edema</u> (most often ankle <u>edema</u>)

* <u>Right ventricular hypertrophy</u> with <u>signs of right heart failure</u> and <u>cor pulmonale</u>

* <u>Hepatomegaly</u>

* Often weight loss and <u>cachexia</u>

* <u>Secondary polycythemia</u>

* Confusion: due to <u>hypoxemia</u> and <u>hypercapnia</u>

* <u>Nail clubbing</u> in the case of certain comorbidities (e.g., <u>bronchiectasis</u>, <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>, <u>lung cancer</u>) [[15]](/library/8VYOwL)





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Nail clubbing</u> is not a finding specific to COPD; its presence usually suggests comorbidities such as <u>bronchiectasis</u>, <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>, or <u>lung cancer</u>.




### Pink puffer and blue bloater [[14]](/library/FVYgwL)




According to their clinical appearance, patients with COPD are often categorized as either “<u>Pink Puffer</u>” or “<u>Blue Bloater</u>”.




| Pink puffer vs. blue bloater |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Pink Puffer | Blue Bloater |
| Main pathomechanism | <br>* <u>Emphysema</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Chronic bronchitis</u><br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br><br>* Noncyanotic<br><br>* Cachectic<br><br>* Pursed-lip breathing<br><br>* Mild <u>cough</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Productive <u>cough</u><br><br>* <u>Overweight</u><br><br>* <u>Peripheral edema</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> | <br>* Slightly reduced<br><br> | <br>* Markedly reduced<br><br> |
| <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u> | <br>* Normal (possibly in late <u>hypercapnia</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Increased (early <u>hypercapnia</u>)<br><br> |





![Facial features in chronic bronchitis](media/penet7chlpu3c63vuoq4qinh.jpg)

Facial features in chronic bronchitis




### Features of COPD due to <u>AATD</u>




* Age of onset is generally younger (< 60 years)

* Also, often have hepatic signs and symptoms (<u>jaundice</u>) related to <u>hepatitis</u> or <u>cirrhosis</u>

## Subtypes and variants

### <u>Emphysema</u> subtypes




<u>Emphysema</u> is characterized by the destruction of <u>lung parenchyma</u> and is often seen in patients with advanced pulmonary disease. The presence of <u>emphysema</u> does not necessarily correlate with spirometric findings. <u>Emphysema</u> can be divided into the following subtypes:   [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)[[16]](/library/HxbKBD)




* Centrilobular emphysema (<u>centriacinar emphysema</u>)  

* Most common type of <u>emphysema</u>

* Classically seen in smokers

* Characterized by the destruction of the <u>respiratory bronchiole</u> (central portion of the acinus); spares <u>distal</u> <u>alveoli</u>

* Usually affects the upper lobes

* Panlobular emphysema (<u>panacinar emphysema</u>)

* Rare type of <u>emphysema</u>

* Associated with <u>AATD</u>

* Characterized by the destruction of the entire acinus (<u>respiratory bronchiole</u> and <u>alveoli</u>)

* Usually affects the lower lobes

* Other subtypes

* Cicatricial emphysema

* Mainly caused by exposure to quartz dust

* Results in <u>chronic inflammation</u> and nodular <u>scar</u> formation

* Giant bullous emphysema

* Characterized by large <u>bullae</u> (congenital or acquired) that extrude into the surrounding tissue

* <u>Bullae</u> may rupture, leading to <u>pneumothorax</u>.

* Depending on the shape of the <u>bullae</u>, resection should be considered.

* Age-related emphysema

* Loss of pulmonary elasticity with age may lead to an <u>emphysematous</u> <u>lung</u>.

* Considered a normal consequence of <u>aging</u>





> [!NOTE]
> “Smoke rises up:” Centriacinar <u>emphysema</u> is associated with smoking and primarily involves the upper lobes of the <u>lungs</u>.

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




* Suspect COPD in patients with either:

* Typical <u>symptoms of COPD</u>

* <u>COPD risk factors</u>

* Obtain <u>spirometry</u> to confirm significant airflow limitation (<u>FEV<sub>1</sub>:FVC</u> < 70%).

* Screen for <u>AATD</u>.

* Consider additional diagnostic testing as indicated, e.g.:

* Advanced <u>PFTs</u>

* Chest imaging





> [!TIP]
> The <u>USPSTF</u> recommends against screening asymptomatic adults for COPD. The GOLD guideline recommends screening with <u>spirometry</u> in patients undergoing annual <u>lung cancer screening</u> with <u>low-dose CT scans</u> and patients with incidental imaging findings consistent with COPD. [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)[[17]](/library/WSWPAk0)




### Initial tests [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)[[2]](/library/kIYm1q)




* <u>Spirometry</u>  

* <u>FEV<sub>1</sub>:FVC</u> < 70% after <u>bronchodilator</u> inhalation confirms the diagnosis.

* ↓ <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> (<u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> % of the predicted value determines the GOLD spirometric grade.)

* Normal or ↓ <u>FVC</u>

* Serum <u>AAT</u> level: Screen all patients with confirmed COPD for <u>AATD</u> upon initial diagnosis.





> [!NOTE]
> “A COP with low <u>FEV</u>er”: <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> for COPD patients.




### Additional testing




#### Advanced <u>pulmonary function testing</u>




Characteristic changes are observed in patients with significant <u>emphysema</u> and small <u>airway</u> abnormalities.




* <u>Body plethysmography</u> 

* ↑ <u>Total lung capacity</u> (TLC)

* ↑ <u>Functional residual capacity</u> (<u>FRC</u>)

* ↑ <u>Residual volume</u> (RV)

* <u>Single-breath diffusing capacity</u>: ↓ <u>DL<sub>CO</sub></u>

* <u>Postbronchodilator test</u>: A negative response (change in <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> < 12%) is more common in patients with COPD than <u>asthma</u> (see “<u>COPD vs. asthma</u>”).  [[18]](/library/fJ1kt30)[[19]](/library/D611M30)





> [!TIP]
> Reversibility of bronchoconstriction is not a reliable factor for differentiating between COPD and <u>asthma</u>. [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)

#### Assessment for <u>respiratory failure</u>




* <u>Pulse oximetry</u>

* Obtain in patients with <u>signs of respiratory distress</u> or <u>signs of right heart failure</u>.

* Measure at rest and on ambient air or usual oxygen prescription.

* <u>ABG</u>

* Obtain in patients with <u>SO<sub>2</sub></u> < 92% and/or acute illness (e.g., <u>altered mental status</u>, <u>AECOPD</u>).

* Findings

* May show <u>hypoxemic respiratory failure</u> (↓ PO<sub>2</sub>) with or without <u>hypercapnic respiratory failure</u> (↑ <u>PCO<sub>2</sub></u>)

* Chronic <u>hypercapnia</u> due to CO<sub>2</sub>trapping is common in patients with severe COPD.





#### Chest imaging [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)[[2]](/library/kIYm1q)




Chest imaging is not needed for diagnosis; consider based on clinical context to assess for alternative diagnoses, comorbidities, or complications.




* Chest x-ray findings in COPD 

* Signs of <u>pulmonary hyperinflation</u>

* Increased <u>anteroposterior diameter</u>;  (barrel chest)

* Pushed down and flattened <u>diaphragm</u>

* Horizontal <u>ribs</u> and widened <u>intercostal spaces</u>

* Hyperlucency of <u>lung tissue</u> (decreased <u>lung markings</u>)

* Long and narrow <u>heart</u> shadow

* Signs of <u>bullous</u> <u>emphysema</u>: <u>parenchymal</u> <u>bullae</u> or <u>pulmonary blebs</u>

* CT chest findings

* Similar to <u>CXR</u> findings; may additionally reveal characteristic patterns of <u>emphysema</u>  

* <u>Panacinar emphysema</u>: common in patients with <u>AATD</u>

* <u>Centriacinar emphysema</u>: common in patients with COPD and a history of tobacco use

* May show signs of <u>bronchiectasis</u>, e.g., thickened bronchial walls

#### Other




* <u>CBC</u> [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)

* <u>Secondary polycythemia</u>, ↑ <u>hematocrit</u>

* <u>Eosinophil</u> counts may be used to guide decisions on management of <u>inhaled corticosteroids</u>. [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)

* <u>ECG</u>/<u>TTE</u>: <u>Right ventricular hypertrophy</u> may be seen in patients with advanced COPD. [[20]](/library/vWbAMs)

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Asthma</u> (see “<u>Comparison of asthma and COPD</u>”)

* <u>Heart failure</u>

* <u>Bronchiectasis</u>

* <u>Tuberculosis</u>

* <u>Bronchiolitis</u>

* See also “<u>Differential diagnosis of chronic cough</u>.”




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

<u>Management of acute COPD exacerbation</u> is discussed in <u>AECOPD</u>.




### Approach [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




* Assess for both:

* Symptom severity and history of exacerbations to determine the <u>GOLD group</u>

* Comorbidities that may influence treatment, e.g., <u>asthma</u>

* Provide <u>nonpharmacological management of COPD</u> for all patients.

* Initiate <u>pharmacological treatment of COPD</u> based on <u>GOLD group</u>.

* At follow-up:

* Review inhaler technique.

* Adjust medication based on the adequacy of symptom control.

* Repeat <u>spirometry</u> annually to track any decline in <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u>.

* In patients with advanced disease, consider:

* <u>Long-term oxygen therapy</u>

* Interventional treatment, e.g., <u>lung volume reduction surgery</u>





### Nonpharmacological management of COPD [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




#### Lifestyle modifications




* Counsel on <u>smoking cessation</u> and options for pharmacotherapy, e.g., <u>varenicline</u>.

* Encourage physical activity to reduce the risk of acute exacerbations.

* Recommend maintenance of a healthy <u>nutritional status</u>.

* Educate patients on:

* Indoor <u>air pollution</u> mitigation, e.g., nonpolluting cooking stoves

* <u>Personal protective equipment</u> to prevent <u>work-related lung diseases</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Tobacco smoking cessation</u> is the single most effective step to slow the decline in <u>lung function</u> in patients with COPD.




#### <u>Supportive care</u>




* Recommended immunizations in COPD

* <u>Influenza vaccination</u> (annual)

* <u>Pneumococcal vaccination</u>: for patients ≥ 19 years of age [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)

* <u>COVID-19 vaccination</u>

* <u>Tdap vaccination</u>: if not administered in <u>adolescence</u>

* <u>Zoster vaccination</u>: for patients > 50 years of age [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)

* <u>RSV vaccination</u>: for patients ≥ 60 years of age and/or with chronic <u>lung</u> or <u>heart</u> disease [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)

* See also “<u>ACIP immunization schedule</u>.”

* <u>Pulmonary rehabilitation</u>: especially helpful for patients with moderate to severe disease





> [!TIP]
> <u>Vaccinations</u> against <u>pneumococcus</u> and <u>influenza</u> reduce the risk of respiratory infections and complications in patients with COPD. [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




#### Management of comorbidities




Screen for common comorbidities at the first visit and at regular intervals, then treat as indicated.




* <u>Screening for depression</u> and <u>anxiety</u>

* <u>Screening for osteoporosis</u>

* <u>ASCVD risk assessment</u>

* Assessment for <u>malnourishment</u>

* <u>Lung cancer screening</u> for patients with COPD resulting from tobacco use

---

## Pharmacological treatment

See “<u>Pharmacotherapy for AECOPD</u>” for treatment of acute exacerbations.




### General principles [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




* <u>Bronchodilators</u> are the mainstay of pharmacological treatment.

* <u>Inhaled corticosteroids</u> (<u>ICS</u>), e.g., <u>budesonide</u>, <u>fluticasone</u>, or <u>beclomethasone</u>, should only be used in combination with long-acting <u>bronchodilators</u>.

* A single inhaler may be more effective than multiple inhalers when available and affordable.

* Patient education on proper inhaler technique is essential for adequate symptom control.

* Describe and demonstrate when prescribing a new inhaler.

* Observe the patient's technique for each inhaler at follow-up visits.

* Identify common errors, e.g., inadequate exhalation prior to inhalation.

* For patients with both COPD and <u>asthma</u>, choose medications based on <u>stepwise treatment of chronic asthma</u>.





### Initial treatment




| <br>Initial pharmacological treatment of stable COPD [[1]](/library/IEdYC70) |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>GOLD group</u> | Daily regimen |  | <u>Rescue medication</u> |  |
| <u>GOLD group A</u> | <br><br>* Long-acting <u>bronchodilator</u> (preferred if available and affordable)<br><br>* <u>Long-acting beta agonist</u> (<u>LABA</u>), e.g., <u>salmeterol</u> DOSAGE, <u>formoterol</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR <u>long-acting muscarinic antagonist</u> (<u>LAMA</u>), e.g., <u>tiotropium bromide</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR consider a <u>rescue medication</u> alone for patients with very occasional <u>dyspnea</u>.<br><br><br> |  | <br>* Short-acting <u>bronchodilator</u> for immediate relief of <u>dyspnea</u><br><br>* <u>Short-acting beta agonist</u> (<u>SABA</u>), e.g., <u>albuterol</u> DOSAGE, <u>levalbuterol</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* Or <u>short-acting muscarinic antagonist</u> (<u>SAMA</u>), e.g., <u>ipratropium bromide</u> DOSAGE<br><br> |  |
| <u>GOLD group B</u> | <br>* <u>LABA</u>/<u>LAMA</u> combination therapy, e.g., <u>umeclidinium</u>/vilanterol DOSAGE<br><br> |  |  |  |
| <u>GOLD group E</u> | <br><br>* <u>LABA</u>/<u>LAMA</u> combination therapy<br><br>* OR, in patients with an <u>eosinophil</u> count â¥ 300/Î¼L, consider <u>LAMA</u>/<u>LABA</u>/<u>ICS</u> triple therapy, e.g., <u>fluticasone</u> furoate/<u>umeclidinium</u>/vilanterol DOSAGE<br><br><br> |  |  |  |
| <br><br>* DPI: dry powdered inhaler<br><br>* <u>MDI</u>: metered dose inhaler<br><br><br> |  |  |  |  |





> [!TIP]
> If treatment response is inadequate, consider poor inhaler technique and/or <u>poor adherence</u> as causes.




![Initial pharmacotherapy for stable COPD](media/pqyltumssdqklcyyo1s8nidc.jpg)

Initial pharmacotherapy for stable COPD




### Follow-up treatment [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




* Maintain inhaler therapy if <u>dyspnea</u> and exacerbations are well controlled with the current regimen.

* If not, assess for:

* Adherence

* Inhaler technique

* Comorbid conditions that could explain symptoms

* Reinforce <u>nonpharmacological management of COPD</u>.

* Adjust treatment based on the predominant trait (i.e., <u>dyspnea</u> or exacerbations), not on the <u>GOLD group</u> at diagnosis.





| <br>Follow-up treatment in COPD [[1]](/library/IEdYC70) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predominant trait | Current treatment | Follow-up treatment |
| Persistent <u>dyspnea</u> | <br><br>* <u>LABA</u> or <u>LAMA</u> monotherapy<br><br>* OR <u>LABA</u>/<u>ICS</u> combination therapy<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>LAMA</u>/<u>LABA</u> combination therapy, e.g., <u>umeclidinium</u>/vilanterol DOSAGE<br><br> |
| <br>* <u>LABA</u>/<u>LAMA</u> combination therapy<br><br> | <br><br>* Consider changing the inhaler or medication within the same class.<br><br>* Evaluate for other <u>causes of dyspnea</u>.<br><br>* Consider adding <u>ensifentrine</u> (if available)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Persistent exacerbations<br> | <br><br>* <u>LABA</u> or <u>LAMA</u> monotherapy<br><br>* OR <u>LABA</u>/<u>ICS</u> combination therapy<br><br><br> | <br>* Escalate based on blood <u>eosinophil</u> count.<br><br>* If < 300/Î¼L: <u>LAMA</u>/<u>LABA</u> combination therapy<br><br>* If â¥ 300/Î¼L: <u>LAMA</u>/<u>LABA</u>/<u>ICS</u> triple therapy, e.g., <u>fluticasone</u> furoate/<u>umeclidinium</u>/vilanterol DOSAGE<br><br> |
| <br>* <u>LABA</u>/<u>LAMA</u> combination therapy<br><br> | <br>* Based on blood <u>eosinophil</u> count<br><br>* If < 100/Î¼L, consider adding either:<br><br>* <u>Macrolide</u> <u>antibiotic</u>, e.g., <u>azithromycin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)<br><br>* <u>PDE4 inhibitor</u>, e.g., <u>roflumilast</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* If â¥ 100/Î¼L: Add <u>ICS</u> to the regimen, e.g., <u>budesonide</u> DOSAGE OR change to <u>LAMA</u>/<u>LABA</u>/<u>ICS</u> triple therapy, e.g., <u>fluticasone</u> furoate/<u>umeclidinium</u>/vilanterol DOSAGE<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>LABA</u>/<u>LAMA</u>/<u>ICS</u> triple therapy<br><br> | <br><br>* Consider adding either:<br><br>* <u>Macrolide</u> <u>antibiotic</u><br><br>* <u>PDE4 inhibitor</u><br><br>* <u>IL-4</u> <u>receptor</u> alpha <u>antagonist</u>, e.g., <u>dupilumab</u>  [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)<br><br>* Consider stopping or reducing the <u>ICS</u> dose if there are adverse effects, e.g., <u>pneumonia</u>.<br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> Follow-up treatment adjustments are based on treatable traits (<u>dyspnea</u> and frequency of exacerbations) and are made irrespective of the patient's <u>GOLD group</u> (A, B, or, E) at diagnosis. [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




### Other drugs [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




* <u>Methylxanthines</u> (e.g., <u>theophylline</u>)

* Nonselectively antagonize <u>adenosine</u> <u>receptors</u> and inhibit <u>phosphodiesterase</u>

* May be trialed if other <u>bronchodilators</u> are not available

* Unproven benefit

* <u>Mucolytics</u> (e.g., <u>N-acetylcysteine</u>, erdosteine)

* Liquefy mucus by reducing the <u>disulfide bonds</u> of mucoproteins

* Can be useful in reducing exacerbations in certain patients





> [!TIP]
> There is insufficient evidence to support treating stable COPD with <u>antitussives</u>, <u>vasodilators</u>, or <u>leukotriene</u> <u>antagonists</u>. [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)

## Management of advanced disease

### <u>Respiratory support</u> [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




* Long-term oxygen therapy (<u>LTOT</u>)

* Indications

* <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> â¤ 55 mm Hg or <u>SaO<sub>2</sub></u> ≤ 88% at rest despite optimal medication

* OR <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> 55–60 mm Hg in patients with <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>, <u>CHF</u>, or <u>polycythemia</u>

* <u>Target oxygen saturation</u>: > 90%

* Recommended duration: <u>continuous oxygen therapy</u> for ≥ 15 hours/day

* Reevaluate after 60–90 days (with <u>ABG</u> or <u>pulse oximetry</u>).

* Ventilatory support

* <u>Continuous positive airway pressure</u> is useful in patients with COPD and <u>obstructive sleep apnea</u>.

* Long-term <u>noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation</u> may be considered in select patients with severe chronic <u>hypercapnia</u>.





> [!TIP]
> For patients started on <u>LTOT</u>, check blood gasses frequently (with <u>ABG</u> or <u>VBG</u>) to ensure adequate oxygenation without unintended <u>acidosis</u> and <u>CO<sub>2</sub> retention</u>. [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




> [!TIP]
> <u>LTOT</u> increases survival in patients with severe resting <u>hypoxemia</u>.




### Invasive treatment




* Surgical <u>bullectomy</u>: indicated in severe <u>emphysema</u> with hyperinflation and large <u>bullae</u>

* <u>Lung</u> volume reduction

* Indicated for severe <u>emphysema</u> and hyperinflation without large <u>bullae</u>

* Severely affected <u>emphysematous</u> areas of the <u>lung</u> are removed either surgically (<u>lung volume reduction surgery</u>) or endoscopically

* <u>Lung transplantation</u>: may be indicated for very severe COPD, patients not eligible for <u>bullectomy</u> or <u>lung</u> volume reduction, and those with surgical contraindications





### <u>Palliative care</u> [[1]](/library/IEdYC70)




* Optimize <u>nonpharmacological management of COPD</u>

* Offer palliative symptom control for all patients with inadequate relief from optimal medical therapy, e.g.:

* <u>Palliative pharmacotherapy for breathlessness</u>

* Mind-body interventions (e.g., <u>mindfulness practice</u>)

* Initiate early discussion regarding <u>end-of-life care</u> and <u>hospice</u> wishes.





> [!TIP]
> Palliative measures (e.g., low-dose <u>opiates</u>, fans blowing onto the patient's face, or <u>acupuncture</u>) can be used if distressing <u>breathlessness</u> persists despite optimal medical therapy. [[21]](/library/Ga1BN20)[[22]](/library/Ba1z520)

---

## Complications

* Chronic respiratory failure [[6]](/library/U30b3f)

* Long-standing partial <u>respiratory failure</u> (PO<sub>2</sub> at rest < 60 mm Hg)

* <u>Hypoxemic</u> and <u>hypercapnic respiratory failure</u> (PO<sub>2</sub> at rest < 60 mm Hg and <u>PCO<sub>2</sub></u> > 45 mm Hg)

* Occurs in advanced COPD due to progressive <u>emphysematous</u> changes and loss of <u>diffusion</u> surface area

* <u>Acute exacerbation of COPD</u>

* <u>Cor pulmonale</u> (<u>right heart failure</u>)

* <u>Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax</u> due to rupture of <u>bullae</u> (especially in <u>bullous</u> <u>emphysema</u>)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prognosis

* 40–70% of all COPD patients survive the first 5 years after diagnosis. [[23]](/library/9CYN8r)

* Survival rates vary significantly depending on the severity of the disease. [[23]](/library/9CYN8r)

* The <u>BODE index</u> (Body mass, Obstruction, <u>Dyspnea</u>, Exercise) estimates prognosis in patients with COPD. [[24]](/library/vEdAx70)

* Measures that improve survival

* Cessation of tobacco use

* <u>Long-term oxygen therapy</u> in patients with severe resting <u>hypoxemia</u>

* COPD is the third most common <u>cause of death</u> worldwide. [[25]](/library/JVYsvL)
